details:
**Justin Trudeau**
The Liberal Party leader who became Canada's prime minister in 2015, governing from the capital, Ottawa. He is the son of former prime minister Pierre Trudeau and is the most common giveaway for this country in current events questions.

**"Freedom Convoy" and the Emergencies Act**
In early 2022, truckers and supporters protesting COVID-19 vaccine mandates occupied downtown Ottawa and blockaded border crossings. Trudeau responded by declaring a national public order emergency under the Emergencies Act, the first time that law had ever been used.

**James Smith Cree Nation stabbings**
In September 2022, the worst mass stabbing in Canadian history took place on the James Smith Cree Nation and in the nearby village of Weldon in Saskatchewan, killing 11 people. Brothers Myles and Damien Sanderson were the suspects, and the attacks took place at 13 separate locations; Damien was found dead and Myles died in police custody soon after his arrest.

**Jagmeet Singh and the New Democratic Party (NDP)**
Jagmeet Singh is the leader of the left-leaning New Democratic Party, one of Canada's major national parties. When photos of Trudeau in blackface and brownface surfaced in 2019, including one from a school yearbook, Singh said they showed a "pattern of behavior."

**Bloc Québécois**
A federal political party that runs candidates only in Quebec and supports Quebec sovereignty. It is a frequent clue for Canada's party system alongside the Liberals, Conservatives, and NDP.

**Pierre Trudeau and the October Crisis**
Pierre Trudeau was prime minister for most of the period from 1968 to 1984. In the 1970 October Crisis, the Quebec separatist group FLQ kidnapped British diplomat James Cross and Quebec minister Pierre Laporte, and Trudeau used the War Measures Act during peacetime, famously saying "just watch me" when asked how far he would go.

**"Fuddle duddle" and the "walk in the snow"**
Two famous Pierre Trudeau episodes. In 1971 he was accused of swearing in the House of Commons and claimed he had only said "fuddle duddle," and in 1984 he said he decided to retire after a long walk in the snow.

**Residential schools and Pope Francis's visit**
In 2021, possible unmarked graves were found with ground-penetrating radar at former residential schools, church-run boarding schools that Indigenous children had been forced to attend. In July 2022, Pope Francis visited Canada on what he called a "penitential pilgrimage" to apologize for the Catholic Church's role in the schools.

**Whisky War and Hans Island**
A long and mostly friendly dispute with Denmark over tiny Hans Island between Greenland and Canada's Ellesmere Island, in which the two sides took turns leaving bottles of liquor on the island. In June 2022, the countries agreed to split the island, giving Canada a land border with Denmark.

**Meng Wanzhou**
The chief financial officer of the Chinese tech company Huawei, nicknamed the "Princess of Huawei." She was arrested in Vancouver in 2018 on a U.S. extradition request and released in 2021 after reaching a deal with U.S. prosecutors.

**September 2021 snap election and the gravel incident**
Trudeau called an early federal election for September 2021, and the Liberals won another minority government. During a campaign stop in London, Ontario, a protester threw gravel at him.

**Pierre Poilievre**
A politician elected leader of Canada's Conservative Party in 2022. He was criticized for promoting Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as a way to "opt out of inflation."

**Julie Payette**
A former astronaut who served as Governor General, the representative of the British monarch in Canada. She resigned in January 2021 after a review found she had created a toxic workplace and mistreated her staff.

**William Amos**
A Liberal member of Parliament from Quebec who in 2021 was accidentally seen naked on camera during a virtual session of the House of Commons. Weeks later, he was caught on camera urinating during another virtual session.

**Fairy Creek protests**
Protests and blockades on Vancouver Island in British Columbia against a logging company cutting old-growth forest in the Fairy Creek watershed. They led to more than a thousand arrests, among the largest acts of civil disobedience in Canadian history.
